theory.summary: Great drawing starts from the shoulder, not the wrist. Ghosting your stroke above the paper builds muscle memory before the pencil touches down.
key_points: Lock your wrist and pivot from the shoulder for long, straight, energetic strokes.
Plot two light endpoints, ghost the motion 3 times in the air, then commit in one smooth pass.
Vary line weight: heavier marks imply shadow or foreground; lighter marks imply light or distance.
theory.warmup_drill: Fill one page with 20 superimposed straight lines between dots, 10 clean C-curves, and 10 smooth S-curves without slowing down mid-stroke.

concept_images.caption: Shoulder-driven ghosted lines vs. hesitant wrist-drawn 'hairy' lines.

exercise.instructions: Draw 12 varied geometric silhouettes and contour profiles using single-pass ghosted lines. Focus on crisp corners and clean line weight shifts toward the shadow side of the sphere.

theory.summary: An ellipse is simply a circle seen in perspective. Its minor axis always aligns with the cylinder's central spine.
key_points: Draw ellipses in one continuous loop from the shoulder, tracing through twice lightly.
The minor axis splits the ellipse symmetrically and points down the cylinder's center.
Ellipses widen (higher degree) as they move farther below or above your eye level.
theory.warmup_drill: Draw 3 horizontal rows of ellipses changing from narrow (15°) to wide (60°), marking each minor axis.

concept_images.caption: Minor axis alignment and ellipse degree widening away from the horizon.

exercise.instructions: Construct 8 cylinders at varying tilts and eye levels. Draw through the far side of every ellipse lightly so the top and bottom feel grounded in 3D space.

days.title: The 5 Value Zones & Light on Form

theory.summary: Value—not outline—makes 2D shapes feel sculptural. Every lit rounded form follows the same predictable 5-zone light logic.
key_points: Separate the light family (highlight + halftone) cleanly from the shadow family (core + reflected + cast).
The core shadow sits along the terminator where the form turns away from the key light.
Reflected light inside the shadow must never be brighter than your darkest halftone.
theory.warmup_drill: Create a smooth 5-step value scale from paper white to 90% dark graphite, then shade a small 3-inch sphere.

concept_images.caption: Highlight, Halftone, Core Shadow, Reflected Light, and Cast Shadow.

exercise.instructions: Complete two full value studies of the sphere and cone. Use the Grayscale toggle in the viewer to check value relationships and keep shadow shapes unified.

theory.summary: In 1-point perspective, one face of every box stays parallel to the picture plane while depth edges converge to a single vanishing point on the horizon.
key_points: The horizon line always equals the viewer's eye level.
Verticals remain strictly vertical and horizontals stay parallel to the horizon.
All receding depth lines converge toward the single Vanishing Point (VP).
theory.warmup_drill: Draw a horizon line with one center VP and construct 6 transparent boxes above, on, and below eye level.

concept_images.caption: Horizon line, single vanishing point, and receding orthogonal rays.

exercise.instructions: Draw the receding architectural colonnade in 1-point perspective. Establish the eye level first, place repeating pillars using diagonal spacing, then shade the shadow planes.

theory.summary: When a box turns at an angle to you, both sets of horizontal edges recede toward separate left and right vanishing points on the horizon.
key_points: Start by placing the closest vertical corner edge facing the viewer.
Keep left and right VPs spaced comfortably wide—too close causes fisheye distortion.
Every vertical remains perpendicular to the horizon line.
theory.warmup_drill: Draw 5 rotating 2-point boxes along a wide page, varying how much of the left vs. right side face is visible.

concept_images.caption: Rotated box converging to VP-Left and VP-Right on the horizon.

exercise.instructions: Study the rotated studio cube in 2-point perspective, then construct a stacked cluster of 4 interlocking blocks resting on the same ground plane with consistent cast shadows.

theory.summary: Looking sharply up or down tilts verticals toward a third vanishing point above (worm's-eye) or below (bird's-eye) the horizon.
key_points: Use 3-point perspective for monumental scale, skyscrapers, or dramatic camera tilts.
The third VP sits far above or below the horizon along the viewer's center of vision.
Subtle convergence looks heroic; extreme convergence feels dizzying.
theory.warmup_drill: Sketch 4 tall monolith boxes from a low worm's-eye angle converging upward to a high 3rd VP.

concept_images.caption: Three vanishing points creating upward convergence for heroic scale.

exercise.instructions: Draw the 3-point monolith towers from a low angle. Establish all three vanishing points lightly, carve out recessed ledges, and render crisp architectural shadow planes.

theory.summary: Complex objects—from teapots to human heads—are built by combining and intersecting spheres, boxes, cylinders, and cones.
key_points: Draw through overlapping forms so you feel where one volume sits behind or penetrates another.
Use wrapping contour lines (cross-contours) to show surface curvature.
Group cast shadows together so forms feel anchored to the same table plane.
theory.warmup_drill: Draw 4 pairs of intersecting primitives (sphere + box, cylinder + cone) with wrap-around intersection seams.

concept_images.caption: Cross-contour wrapping lines revealing how intersecting forms occupy 3D space.

exercise.instructions: Week 1 Synthesis: Draw and fully shade the overlapping still-life trio (sphere, cylinder, cube). Focus on accurate proportions, clean overlaps, and unified 5-zone lighting.

theory.summary: Construct a sphere, slice off the sides, and establish the brow line, centerline, and jaw plane so the head rotates effortlessly in 3D.
key_points: Start with a light, confident sphere representing the cranial mass.
Slice off roughly 1/6th of each side to form the flat temple planes.
Wrap the brow line around the equator and drop the jaw wedge from the cross-axis.
theory.warmup_drill: Draw 6 quick 90-second Loomis spheres with temple ellipses, brow lines, and centerlines tilted in different directions.

concept_images.caption: 4-step construction of the Loomis head in 3/4 view.

exercise.instructions: Draw 8 Loomis heads tilted at different angles (front, 3/4 up, 3/4 down, profile) without facial features—focus purely on solid planar structure and tilt.

theory.summary: The rule of thirds anchors facial features cleanly on the front plane: hairline to brow, brow to nose base, and nose base to chin.
key_points: Three equal vertical thirds span hairline → brow → bottom of nose → bottom of chin.
Eyes sit roughly halfway between the top of the skull and the chin, spaced one eye-width apart.
Ears align cleanly between the brow line and the base of the nose on the side plane.
theory.warmup_drill: Subdivide 3 front and 3 profile head templates into equal thirds and place eye, nose, mouth, and ear landmarks.

concept_images.caption: Vertical facial thirds and horizontal eye-width alignment guides.

exercise.instructions: Using the front and profile planar references, construct 4 proportionally balanced heads with accurate ear, brow, nose-base, mouth-line, and chin placements.

theory.summary: Eyes are not flat stickers—they are spheres recessed inside a shadowed bony socket, wrapped by thick upper and lower eyelids.
key_points: Carve the recessed keystone/orbital shadow cavity before placing the eyeball sphere.
Wrap the upper and lower eyelids around the curvature of the sphere.
Show eyelid thickness and cast a crisp shadow from the upper lid onto the iris.
theory.warmup_drill: Draw 6 large eyeball spheres at different gazes and wrap upper/lower eyelid ribbons around them.

concept_images.caption: Eyelid ribbons wrapping around the spherical eyeball inside the brow socket.

exercise.instructions: Complete 4 detailed planar and shaded studies of the eye socket, focusing on the transition from the brow ridge down into the orbital shadow and curved lids.

theory.summary: Simplify the nose into a 4-plane prism/wedge and wrap the lips around the cylindrical dental barrel of the jaw.
key_points: The nose has a top bridge, two angled side planes, and a shadowed underside plane.
The mouth wraps around a curved cylinder—the far corner foreshortens in 3/4 view.
The upper lip usually catches shadow while the lower lip catches top light.
theory.warmup_drill: Draw 5 simple wedge noses and 5 cylindrical mouth barrels from front, 3/4, and worm's-eye angles.

concept_images.caption: 4-plane wedge nose and lips wrapping the curved dental cylinder.

exercise.instructions: Draw 4 studies combining the wedge nose and cylindrical mouth planes. Emphasize the underside shadow of the nose and the core shadow beneath the lower lip.

theory.summary: Lighting direction transforms mood. Organizing the head into two clear value shapes—lit vs. shadow—gives portraits instant sculptural power.
key_points: Rembrandt lighting (45°) leaves a small triangular catchlight on the shadow-side cheek.
Split lighting (90°) divides the face sharply along the centerline into light and dark.
Rim lighting carves a bright silhouette edge out of a dark background.
theory.warmup_drill: Draw 3 small thumbnail Loomis heads and block in pure 2-value shadow shapes for Rembrandt, Split, and Rim light.

concept_images.caption: Rembrandt 45°, Split 90°, and Back/Rim portrait lighting patterns.

exercise.instructions: Create three 15-minute value studies comparing Rembrandt, Split, and Rim lighting. Toggle Grayscale in the viewer to verify your light/shadow separation.

theory.summary: Emotion lives in the eyebrows, eyelids, and cheeks squashing or stretching the underlying facial mask while the rigid skull stays unchanged.
key_points: The cranium and teeth never squash or stretch—only the brows, cheeks, and jaw pivot.
Joy pushes cheeks up into the lower eyelids; surprise drops the jaw and lifts the brow.
Anger compresses the inner brow down into the nose bridge.
theory.warmup_drill: Sketch 6 quick expressive thumbnails (joy, surprise, anger, skepticism, calm, sorrow) using simplified brow + mouth masks.

concept_images.caption: Jaw pivot and cheek compression driving clear facial expressions.

exercise.instructions: Use the 3/4 head references as structural armatures to draw 4 expressive character heads (joy, focus, surprise, determination), keeping the underlying Loomis construction solid.

theory.summary: Combine Loomis construction, proportional thirds, recessed features, and unified 2-value lighting into one complete portrait study.
key_points: Work big-to-small: head silhouette → tilt/thirds → shadow shapes → feature details.
Squint often to check that dark accents (nostrils, pupils, mouth corners) stay inside the value hierarchy.
Keep hard edges around focal points (eyes) and softer edges along the jawline and hair.
theory.warmup_drill: Do a 5-minute thumbnail value block-in of the Rembrandt head using only 2 tones before starting the main drawing.

concept_images.caption: Big-to-small portrait workflow: block-in, shadow map, then focal refinement.

exercise.instructions: Week 2 Synthesis: Spend the full 45 minutes completing a polished, rendered planar portrait study using the Rembrandt lighting reference.

theory.summary: Gesture is not an outline—it is the energy, rhythm, and balance running through the pose. Capture the whole figure in seconds using sweeping C- and S-curves.
key_points: Find one primary Line of Action flowing from the head through the spine to the weight-bearing foot.
Draw the action first with long rhythmic curves—never trace contours bead-by-bead.
Contrast a stretched side against a compressed pinch side to make poses feel alive.
theory.warmup_drill: Draw 10 ultra-fast 30-second stick-and-ribbon gesture lines capturing only spine curve, shoulder tilt, and hip tilt.

concept_images.caption: Sweeping C/S-curve line of action with opposing shoulder and hip tilts.

exercise.instructions: Timed Gesture Interval Session: Run the 60-second Interval Timer in the fullscreen viewer. Each time it chimes, it automatically advances to the next pose—keep your pencil moving continuously!

theory.summary: Two primary rigid masses—the egg-shaped ribcage and wedge-shaped pelvis—drive almost every twist, bend, and weight shift of the human figure.
key_points: Simplify the ribcage as an upright egg and the pelvis as a compact rounded box/bucket.
When one side of the waist stretches, the opposite side pinches into soft folds.
Mark the centerline (sternum to navel) and spinal furrow to show 3D rotation.
theory.warmup_drill: Draw 8 floating 'beans' bending, twisting, and leaning without limbs.

concept_images.caption: Ribcage ovoid and pelvis block creating pinch and stretch along the waist.

exercise.instructions: Study the front torso bean and back torso scapulae references. Draw 6 three-quarter torso constructions from multiple angles with clear centerline wrapping.

theory.summary: Using the head as a modular ruler (7.5 to 8 heads tall) keeps limbs, torso, and center of gravity aligned without stiff measuring.
key_points: Halfway mark of an 8-head standing figure sits right at the hip/pubic bone.
Elbows align roughly with the waist/navel; wrists reach mid-hip/upper thigh.
Drop a vertical plumb line from the pit of the neck to check balance over the supporting foot.
theory.warmup_drill: Rule an 8-head vertical grid and map key landmarks (chin, nipples, navel, hip, mid-thigh, knees, ankles).

concept_images.caption: 8-head proportional canon and vertical balance plumb line.

exercise.instructions: Draw 3 full standing figures (front, contrapposto, and stride) checking your 8-head landmarks and plumb-line weight distribution.

theory.summary: When a limb points toward or away from the viewer, its length compresses while overlapping T-junctions and contour ellipses carry all the depth.
key_points: Think in stacked coils/cylinders rather than flat outlines.
Closer cylinders overlap farther ones with bold T-junction lines.
Wrap cross-contour ellipses around the arm or thigh to show whether it aims toward or away from you.
theory.warmup_drill: Draw 4 foreshortened Slinky-like cylinder chains aiming directly toward your nose.

concept_images.caption: Stacked cylinder rings and T-junction overlaps creating instant depth.

exercise.instructions: Draw 4 studies of the foreshortened reaching arm and athletic lunge pose, emphasizing large foreground overlap and compressed limb length.

theory.summary: Limbs are rhythmic chains of tapered cylinders with alternating curves—straight vs. curved—creating natural anatomical grace.
key_points: Every limb segment follows the 'straight against curve' rhythm (e.g., straight shin bone vs. curved calf).
Upper arm and thigh taper down toward narrower elbow and knee joints.
Use simple block joints so wrists and ankles connect cleanly.
theory.warmup_drill: Draw 6 pairs of upper/lower arms and legs as tapered cylinders with opposing rhythmic curves.

concept_images.caption: Tapered limb cylinders with alternating straight-vs-curve rhythm.

exercise.instructions: Break down the striding and reaching mannequin poses into clean, shaded tapered cylinders and spherical hinge joints.

theory.summary: Hands and feet intimidate beginners only when drawn finger-by-finger. Group them into simple palm boxes, mitten shapes, and wedges first.
key_points: Block the palm as a slightly arched pentagon/box before adding finger cylinders.
Group the four fingers into a unified mitten silhouette, then split knuckles along gentle arcs.
Build feet from an ankle cylinder dropping into a triangular wedge + toe box.
theory.warmup_drill: Draw 5 palm-box mittens and 5 triangular foot wedges from different angles in 10 minutes.

concept_images.caption: Palm box, knuckle arc, and segmented cylinder fingers.
Ankle cylinder resting on a triangular arch wedge.

exercise.instructions: Complete 3 block-construction hand studies and 3 shaded foot wedge studies, plus 2 studies of your own non-drawing hand from life.

theory.summary: Unite gesture energy, torso bean volume, 8-head proportions, cylinder limbs, and unified lighting into one finished figure study.
key_points: Minutes 1–5: Gesture line of action + weight balance.
Minutes 5–20: Torso bean, head tilt, and cylinder limbs.
Minutes 20–45: Unified shadow family, core shadows, and crisp anatomical accents.
theory.warmup_drill: Do two 2-minute gesture warmups before committing to your 45-minute full constructed figure.

concept_images.caption: Gesture → Structural Volumes → Unified Value Shading.

exercise.instructions: Week 3 Synthesis: Produce a complete 45-minute shaded figure drawing of the Contrapposto Twist or Seated Forward Lean pose.

theory.summary: Avoid cutting landscapes cleanly in half. Placing the horizon on the upper or lower third immediately declares whether the sky or land is the star.
key_points: Low horizon (bottom third) celebrates dramatic skies and vertical scale.
High horizon (top third) emphasizes grounded foreground paths, water, or terrain.
Place your primary focal landmark near one of the four Rule-of-Thirds intersections.
theory.warmup_drill: Draw 6 tiny 2×3-inch thumbnail frames testing high vs. low horizons with the Grid overlay concept.

concept_images.caption: 3×3 Rule of Thirds intersections and unequal sky-to-land ratios.

exercise.instructions: Open the Coastal Headland reference and toggle the 3×3 Composition Grid in the viewer. Create 3 compositional thumbnails, then render one larger balanced landscape.

theory.summary: Air scatters light over distance: far mountain ridges grow lighter, lower in contrast, and softer in edge compared to bold foreground silhouettes.
key_points: Organize landscapes into distinct Foreground, Midground, and Background planes.
Foreground carries the darkest darks, highest contrast, and sharpest texture.
Distant ridges compress into light, low-contrast pale silhouettes.
theory.warmup_drill: Paint or shade 4 overlapping ridge strips stepping smoothly from 90% foreground dark to 15% background haze.

concept_images.caption: Contrast and value compression across foreground, midground, and background.

exercise.instructions: Draw the 5-layer mountain valley study. Use the Grayscale toggle to check that each receding ridge steps cleanly lighter without overlapping values.

theory.summary: Clouds are weightless 3D puffs obeying the same directional light rules as spheres—lit tops, halftone bellies, and soft lost edges.
key_points: Keep cloud bases flatter in perspective as they recede toward the horizon.
Group big puff masses first before breaking up smaller wispy edges.
Leave crisp edges on the sunlit tops and soft lost edges on shadowed undersides.
theory.warmup_drill: Draw 4 puffy cloud silhouettes using soft side-of-pencil shading and kneaded-eraser lifts.

concept_images.caption: Cumulus clouds treated as overlapping lit spheres with flat perspective bases.

exercise.instructions: Render two full sky-and-cloud studies focusing on smooth sky value gradation and volumetric cloud lighting above a low horizon.

theory.summary: Never draw individual leaves! Treat tree canopies like big rounded clouds of spheres catching directional light and casting deep core shadows.
key_points: Block the entire canopy into 3–5 major overlapping spherical masses.
Unify the shadow side of the foliage before adding any leaf-cluster texture.
Leave small 'sky holes' near canopy edges and taper branches as they split.
theory.warmup_drill: Draw 5 simplified tree silhouettes built from 3 overlapping lit spheres and tapered Y-branches.

concept_images.caption: Grouping foliage into major lit and shadowed canopy masses before texture.

exercise.instructions: Draw 3 full studies of the shaded tree canopy reference, keeping individual leaf marks only along the high-contrast light/shadow border.

theory.summary: Calm water acts like a darkened vertical mirror directly beneath objects, broken only by horizontal ripple strokes.
key_points: Reflections sit vertically straight beneath the object reflecting them.
Darken sunlit sky reflections slightly and lighten dark land reflections slightly.
Keep all ripple strokes strictly horizontal—narrow near the shore, wider in the foreground.
theory.warmup_drill: Sketch a simple lakeside ridge and mirror its silhouette vertically downward with broken horizontal ripple gaps.

concept_images.caption: Vertical reflection alignment broken by horizontal surface ripples.

exercise.instructions: Complete the Lake Reflection study and the Winding Pathway scene to practice horizontal water planes and S-curve compositional lead-ins.

theory.summary: Notan reduces a complex scene to pure black-and-white 2-value design. If a drawing reads well as two shapes, it will hold together at any detail level.
key_points: Turn on Grayscale and squint until midtones disappear into either light or dark.
Link cast shadows together into bold, sweeping abstract shapes.
Save pure paper white and deepest black for your focal zone.
theory.warmup_drill: Draw three 2-minute black-and-white Notan thumbnails (no gray!) of the sunlit alleyway.

concept_images.caption: 2-value Notan simplification uniting cast shadows into one bold dark shape.

exercise.instructions: Create a bold 2-value Notan design of the Sunlit Alleyway, then expand it into a 3-value (Light, Mid, Dark) finished architectural study.

theory.summary: Rocks obey the exact same planar lighting rules as cubes—sharp fractures, flat sunlit tops, and vertical shadowed faces.
key_points: Treat boulders as angular chipped cubes rather than smooth potatoes.
Follow geological strata lines wrapping across the planes to show volume.
Use sharp, angular hatching strokes to convey hard stone texture.
theory.warmup_drill: Sketch 4 angular fractured rock blocks showing distinct top, front, and side value planes.

concept_images.caption: Stratified cliff planes constructed like chipped 2-point blocks.

exercise.instructions: Week 4 Synthesis: Draw the Stratified Rock Cliff Planes, combining bold shadow shapes, planar fractures, and crisp sunlit edges.

theory.summary: Bring together perspective, human scale, and atmospheric depth so a figure feels genuinely placed inside a vast world.
key_points: Place the horizon line carefully: characters standing on flat ground share eye level with the horizon.
Use dark foreground framing elements to push distant valley layers further back.
Keep the focal figure crisp and silhouetted against a bright atmospheric background.
theory.warmup_drill: Sketch 3 thumbnail compositions testing figure placement along Rule-of-Thirds intersections.

concept_images.caption: Framing a scale figure against atmospheric depth using the Rule of Thirds.

exercise.instructions: Capstone Part 1: Choose either Traveler Overlooking the Valley or Monumental Archway & Scale Figure and execute a complete, carefully composed 45-minute drawing.

days.title: Capstone II: Master Value & Mood Study

theory.summary: Day 30 celebrates everything you've practiced—confident lines, solid perspective, believable form lighting, and deliberate mood.
key_points: Commit to one strong light source and protect your light vs. shadow value separation.
Guide the viewer's eye with highest contrast at the focal point and quiet detail elsewhere.
After finishing, upload your Day 30 sketch and compare it side-by-side with Day 1 in My Sketchbook!
theory.warmup_drill: Spend 5 minutes planning your value hierarchy (Lightest Light, Midtone, Darkest Dark) on a small thumbnail.

concept_images.caption: Concentrating highest contrast at the focal point to tell a visual story.

exercise.instructions: Final Capstone Piece: Complete a full 45-minute atmospheric light & mood study of the Sunlit Bust Interior or Dusk Lantern scene. Snap a photo afterward for your Day 1 vs. Day 30 comparison!
